title: Bidirectional Dijkstra on New York (SoHo) ⚡
description: Visualizing Bidirectional Dijkstra pathfinding on New York (SoHo)
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale ⚡—Inside high-scale navigation engines, the “meet-in-the-middle” trick powers faster shortest paths.

Here’s what you’re seeing on Amsterdam’s grid: instead of one Dijkstra wave, we run two—one from the start and one from the destination. Each side expands by lowest current distance, and as soon as their search regions overlap, we stitch the best route through the meeting node. Result: dramatically fewer explored nodes compared to classic single-source search, especially when the path isn’t too long.

Technical takeaway: both searches maintain correct distances; termination happens when the best candidate path cost can’t be improved (based on frontier distances). Same optimality—less exploration.

Debate question: would you rather optimize for fewer expanded nodes (speed) or for simpler implementation (engineering cost)?

Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale ⚡ Inside high-scale navigation engines: Bidirectional Dijkstra visualised for shortest path at scale.

In this Short, we run two Dijkstra frontiers—one expanding from the start and one from the goal—then stop when the searches meet to build the optimal route. You’ll see why this bidirectional strategy explores far fewer nodes than classic single-direction Dijkstra while preserving correctness.
